roas.description: Calculate return on ad spend from attributed revenue and campaign cost. See ROAS as a multiple and percentage, with a worked example and limitations.
roas.intro: Compare the revenue attributed to a campaign with the amount spent on its advertising. Match the date range, attribution model and currency before entering your figures.
roas.formula: ROAS = attributed revenue ÷ advertising spend. ROAS percentage = ROAS × 100.
roas.example: A campaign generates 5,000 in attributed revenue from 1,000 in ad spend. Its ROAS is 5,000 ÷ 1,000 = 5×, equivalent to 500%.
roas.limitations: ROAS is a revenue measure. It excludes product costs, refunds, agency fees, platform fees and overhead unless those are included in your source figures. A high ROAS does not establish that a campaign is profitable.
steps: Enter campaign revenue attributed using one consistent attribution model.
Enter advertising spend for the same campaign and reporting period; spend must be greater than zero.
Calculate to see the revenue multiple and percentage. Reset clears the form for another campaign.

faq.question: Is 5× ROAS the same as a 500% profit?
faq.answer: No. 5× ROAS means five units of revenue for each unit of advertising spend. Calculate profit after all relevant costs separately with the profit margin calculator.

margin.description: Calculate profit and profit margin from revenue and total cost. Understand negative margins and the difference between margin and markup.
margin.intro: Find the profit remaining after your chosen costs, then express it as a share of revenue. Use a single product, order or reporting period consistently.
margin.formula: Profit = revenue − total cost. Profit margin (%) = (revenue − total cost) ÷ revenue × 100.
margin.example: Revenue of 100 and total cost of 60 produce a profit of 40. Profit margin is 40 ÷ 100 × 100 = 40%.
margin.limitations: The result reflects only the costs you enter. Include shipping, returns, advertising and platform fees when relevant. Revenue must be greater than zero; costs above revenue correctly produce a negative margin. This is a planning calculation, not tax or accounting advice.
steps: Enter revenue in your chosen currency for one product, order or reporting period.
Enter all costs relevant to that same scope.
Calculate to see profit and margin. Reset clears the inputs and result.

faq.question: How is profit margin different from markup?
faq.answer: Margin divides profit by revenue; markup divides profit by cost. A product that costs 60 and sells for 100 has a 40% margin and about 66.67% markup.

dpi.description: Check image pixels per inch at a chosen print size in inches or centimeters. Calculate both axes and understand PPI, DPI and aspect-ratio limits.
dpi.intro: Check the horizontal and vertical resolution of an image at its intended physical print size. This measures pixels per inch (PPI), often informally called print DPI.
dpi.formula: Horizontal PPI = image width in pixels ÷ print width in inches. Vertical PPI = image height in pixels ÷ print height in inches. Inches = centimeters ÷ 2.54.
dpi.example: An image measuring 3,000 × 2,400 pixels printed at 10 × 8 inches gives 300 PPI on both axes. The same print size is 25.4 × 20.32 centimeters.
dpi.limitations: Pixel dimensions must be positive whole numbers. PPI describes image sampling, while printer DPI describes ink dots. Around 300 PPI is a common starting point for close-viewed prints, not a universal requirement. Different results on the two axes can indicate a shape mismatch; ask your printer about cropping, stretching, viewing distance and bleed.
steps: Enter the image width and height in pixels from the file properties.
Enter the intended print dimensions and choose inches or centimeters.
Calculate to check both axes. Reset clears your measurements.

faq.question: Does changing a file's DPI metadata create detail?
faq.answer: No. Changing a resolution label does not add image detail. The available pixels and final physical dimensions determine PPI. Upscaling may add pixels, but it cannot recover original detail that was never captured.

cpc.description: Calculate average cost per click from ad spend and clicks. Compare campaign traffic costs using matching periods and consistent attribution.
steps: Enter advertising spend in one currency.
Enter the positive whole-number count of clicks for the same campaign and period.
Calculate the average cost per click, then compare it with the value of your traffic.

faq.question: Does a lower CPC always mean a better campaign?
faq.answer: No. Lower traffic cost can still produce fewer qualified leads or sales. Review conversion rate, CPA and ROAS alongside CPC.

cpm.description: Calculate advertising cost per thousand impressions from spend and served impressions. See the CPM formula and a worked campaign example.
steps: Enter advertising spend in your chosen currency.
Enter the positive whole-number count of impressions for the same reporting period.
Calculate the cost of one thousand impressions; impressions count ad displays, not unique people.

faq.question: Are impressions the same as reach?
faq.answer: No. One person may see an ad several times. CPM uses impressions, while reach estimates distinct people or accounts.

ctr.description: Calculate click-through rate as clicks divided by impressions. Check engagement using consistent campaign and reporting-period counts.
steps: Enter the clicks recorded by your chosen advertising or analytics platform.
Enter impressions measured using the same campaign and reporting window.
Calculate the percentage of impressions that resulted in clicks.

faq.question: Can I compare CTR across every advertising channel?
faq.answer: Use caution. Placements, audience intent and click definitions differ. Compare similar campaigns and confirm the platform's reporting definitions.

cpa.description: Calculate average cost per acquisition or action from campaign spend and conversions. Keep conversion definitions and reporting periods consistent.
steps: Choose the conversion you want to measure, such as a purchase or qualified lead.
Enter campaign spend and the number of those conversions for the same reporting window.
Calculate the average cost of each recorded acquisition or action.

faq.question: Is CPA the same as customer acquisition cost?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. CPA often measures one advertising action. Customer acquisition cost may include sales salaries, software and other acquisition costs in addition to advertising.

discount.description: Calculate a sale price and savings from an original price and percentage discount. Check the price before tax, shipping or other extra charges.
steps: Enter the original price in a single currency.
Enter the percentage discount from zero to one hundred.
Calculate to see the discounted price and the amount saved.

faq.question: Can I add two percentage discounts together?
faq.answer: Successive discounts usually apply to the reduced price. A 20% discount followed by 10% gives a 28% total reduction, not 30%. Calculate each stage separately.

markup.description: Calculate markup percentage and profit from unit cost and selling price. Compare markup on cost with profit margin on revenue.
steps: Enter the cost of the item or service, using the same cost basis throughout.
Enter the selling price in the same currency.
Calculate profit and the percentage markup on cost. Selling below cost produces a negative markup.

faq.question: Why does a 50% markup give less than a 50% margin?
faq.answer: Markup is calculated on cost; margin is calculated on selling price. A cost of 100 marked up by 50% sells for 150, so the margin is 50 ÷ 150 = 33.33%.

break-even.description: Estimate break-even sales units from fixed costs, selling price and variable unit cost. See the contribution-margin formula and whole-unit rounding.
steps: Enter fixed costs for one defined period or project.
Enter selling price per unit and variable cost per unit in the same currency.
Calculate the units needed to cover costs. Use the rounded-up whole-unit result when selling indivisible products.

faq.question: What if variable cost is at least the selling price?
faq.answer: There is no positive contribution available to cover fixed costs. A finite break-even quantity cannot be calculated under that pricing model.

bleed-trim.description: Calculate artwork size from trim dimensions and bleed on each side. Confirm print production dimensions before sending a file to your printer.
steps: Enter the final trimmed width and height in the selected physical unit.
Enter the bleed required on each edge by your print supplier.
Calculate the complete artwork size, and extend the background into the bleed area in your design software.

faq.question: Is bleed the same as a safe text margin?
faq.answer: No. Bleed extends artwork beyond the trim edge. A safe margin keeps essential text and graphics inside the trim edge. Confirm both requirements with your printer.

print-size.description: Convert print dimensions between millimeters, inches and pixels at a chosen PPI. Understand exact physical units and rounded pixel dimensions.
steps: Choose your source unit and enter the image or print dimensions.
Enter the intended image resolution in pixels per inch when converting to or from pixels.
Calculate the equivalent dimensions, then check the final requirements with your print supplier.

faq.question: Why does the converter ask for PPI?
faq.answer: Millimeters and inches are physical units. Pixels describe a digital grid. PPI links that grid to a physical print size; without it there is no single pixel-to-inch conversion.

video-size.description: Estimate video file size from duration and combined bitrate, or estimate bitrate from file size. Understand decimal units and container overhead.
steps: Choose whether to estimate file size or the video bitrate budget.
Enter duration and audio bitrate, then supply either video bitrate or target file size as labeled.
Calculate an estimate and allow additional space for container overhead and encoder variation.

faq.question: Should I include audio bitrate?
faq.answer: Yes. Use the combined average bitrate of the video, audio and any other streams for a closer estimate. Variable bitrate and container overhead can change the final file size.

faq.question: What is the difference between Mbps, MB and MiB?
faq.answer: Mbps measures millions of bits per second. A byte contains eight bits; MB means 1,000,000 bytes and MiB means 1,048,576 bytes. This tool labels its decimal file-size estimate in MB and also shows MiB, so compare like units when checking a download limit.

frames-duration.description: Convert video frames to duration or duration to frame count at a chosen frame rate. Check non-integer frame rates and whole-frame rounding.
steps: Choose frames-to-duration or duration-to-frames.
Enter the frame count or time in seconds, then enter the frame rate used by your project.
Calculate the conversion and check whether whole-frame rounding is suitable for your timeline.

faq.question: Does this convert SMPTE drop-frame timecode?
faq.answer: No. This converts a frame count and elapsed seconds using a constant frame rate. Drop-frame timecode is a separate labeling convention and does not remove video frames.

image-resizer.description: Resize an image in your browser with a local preview and download. Set pixel dimensions and check aspect ratio without uploading your file.
steps: Choose a supported image from your device.
Enter the desired pixel dimensions and choose whether to preserve the aspect ratio.
Process the image, inspect the preview and download the generated file.

faq.question: Will enlarging my image recover missing detail?
faq.answer: No. Browser resizing resamples existing pixels. Enlarging an image can make it softer and does not restore detail that was absent from the original.

image-compressor.description: Compress a supported image locally with JPEG or WebP quality controls. Compare the output size and preview before downloading.
steps: Choose a supported source image from your device.
Select an output format and quality level.
Process the file, compare the output size with the original and download only if the result suits your needs.

faq.question: Why can the compressed image be larger?
faq.answer: A small or already optimized original may encode less efficiently with the selected settings. Check the measured output size; a quality setting cannot guarantee a smaller file.

faq.question: Can I guarantee an output below an exact file-size limit?
faq.answer: No. This tool adjusts encoding quality rather than targeting a specific number of bytes. Process the image, compare the measured output size with your limit and try a lower quality if needed. Dimensions stay the same; use the image resizer first if reducing dimensions is acceptable.

image-converter.description: Convert a supported image to JPEG, PNG or WebP in your browser. Preview the result and understand transparency and metadata limits.
steps: Choose a supported image from your device.
Choose an output format suited to the image and its intended use.
Process the conversion, review the preview and download the result.

faq.question: Which format should I choose?
faq.answer: JPEG is often suitable for photographs; PNG supports lossless output and transparency; WebP can offer smaller files in modern browsers. Conversion may discard metadata and does not preserve animation.

images-to-pdf.description: Create a PDF from supported images locally in your browser. Review page order, output size and image quality before downloading.
steps: Select the supported images you want to include.
Review their order and the available page settings.
Process the images into a PDF and download the generated document.

faq.question: Will this make scanned text searchable?
faq.answer: No. This places image content on PDF pages. It does not perform optical character recognition or turn image text into selectable text.

faq.question: Are my images cropped or kept transparent in the PDF?
faq.answer: Each image is fitted proportionally inside the chosen page margins without cropping. The image is converted to JPEG on a white background, so transparent areas become white. Check the downloaded PDF before printing or sharing it.

pdf-merge.description: Combine supported PDF files locally in your browser. Review file order and download the merged document without a server upload.
steps: Choose the PDF files to combine in the intended order.
Review supported-file and size limits before processing.
Process the merge, download the result and check every page before sharing it.

faq.question: Are signatures and interactive features preserved?
faq.answer: Do not rely on a merge to preserve digital signature validity, interactive forms, attachments or advanced document behavior. Keep the original files and review the output. Encrypted or unsupported PDFs may be rejected.
